title: Kube play: preserve memory-backed emptyDir data after init containers exit
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! -->
I intentionally kept the commits as three commits for easier review. I can later squash with a commit message mentioning the issue as mentioned in the guidelines.

## Problem

[#29555](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29555) reported an
issue with memory-backed `emptyDir` volumes used by `podman kube play`.
[#29565](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/pull/29565) addressed
sharing the tmpfs between regular containers that are running concurrently.
[#29670](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29670) shows the
remaining case: data written by a one-shot init container is unavailable to a
regular container that starts afterward.

<!-- Check that the description of #29565 matches the final merged behavior. -->

## Root cause

A memory-backed `emptyDir` is represented by an anonymous named volume. Podman
mounts a tmpfs at the volume's host-side mountpoint and bind-mounts that path
into the init container.

When a one-shot init container is removed, its volume mounts are released. If
this reduces the volume mount reference count to zero, Podman unmounts the
host-side tmpfs and its contents are lost.

## Approach

The change adds an internal mount of every memory-backed `emptyDir` volume to
the pod's infra container. 

Infra-container mounts are normally inherited by containers subsequently added
to the pod. That behavior supports pod-wide mounts such as:

```console
podman pod create --name mypod --volume myvolume:/data
podman run --pod mypod alpine ls /data
```

I used an additional `NoInherit` option to both `specgen.NamedVolume` and `libpod.ContainerNamedVolume` work around this.


Fixes: #29670
Related: #29555

Hello @magic-peach, 
since you opened the initial PR on this issue, would you mind giving your opinion on this?

LGTM

From a code standpoint.  Could you clean up the Title please a bit, at least remove your branch name?

thanks @devchris123

@TomSweeneyRedHat 
One test failed after my force push. Could you retry that one?

@Honny1 
An alternative approach might be to make the volume lifetime for this particular type of volume explicit. That would require persisting the volume as part of the pod's persistence and tie the lifecycle to the pods lifecycle. E.g. mount the tmpfs on the host upon pod creation and unmount it upon pod removal. But a couple of other failure and edge cases must be considered to ensure the tmpfs is properly cleaned up on partial failures etc.

There are some other problems I found with the current implemenation, which might need fixing in additional commits:
- a tmpfs based PVC also loses data from init-to-app containers
  - I tested this with `podman volume create --opts type=tmpfs <vol-name>`
  - start pod with init and app container
  - write data to the volume in an init container
  - read from the volume from an app container -> data gone
- a pod stop with an image-backed infra container will stop the container and then also unmount the tmpfs effectively losing the data, whereas the default image infra container does not have this behaviour. This is likely incidental
- first-use initialization of a FS could lead to unexpected results, because the infra container touches the volume first (this is not clear to a user) -> this needs further investigation, I haven't checked what mechanism exist

This could be done in this PR or a follow up PR, not inherently blockers I would say.
This PR does not introduce these issues (maybe only change the first-use initialization to some extent, but this remains to be checked)

This isn't the right approach. We should use an anonymous named volume using mount options to make it a tmpfs (from the command line, this would be `podman volume create --opt type=tmpfs --opt device=tmpfs myvol`). This will mimic the K8S behavior properly and doesn't require us to hack in an extra directory for Kubernetes temporary volumes, with all the lifecycle problems that brings
